key_insight: LLMs can answer medical questions correctly at baseline but lose that correctness when exposed to misleading context, revealing weak epistemic resilience.
clinical_relevance: For health-related uses, high exam scores alone may not mean a model will give safe or reliable advice when real-world prompts contain persuasive but false information.
method: Built MedMisBench with 10,932 medical question items and 48,889 misleading context-option pairs.
Tested 11 model configurations across medical reasoning, agentic capability, and patient-journey evaluation.
Measured how often correct answers flipped under deceptive context and how often clinicians judged the cases potentially harmful.
evidence_signal: Mean accuracy dropped from 71.1% on original questions to 38.0% under focused misleading context, with 51.5% attack success and 38.2% of reviewed cases flagged as seriously harmful by clinicians.
watch_item: The benchmark shows susceptibility to adversarial prompting, but real-world performance may vary by model, deployment safeguards, and how closely prompts resemble the benchmark attacks.
paper_title: Measuring Epistemic Resilience of LLMs Under Misleading Medical Context
